One-day itinerary · North London

Highgate: Lost Railway, Ancient Wood and Victorian Cemetery

Follow a railway reclaimed by woodland, detour through an ancient wood, read Highgate’s Victorian landscape and finish above the London skyline.

Nature and infrastructureNorth LondonAny day
Best day
Any day
Duration
09:15–15:50 · about 6 hours 35 minutes
Walking
8.3 km · Active
Transport
No public transport
Balance
Mostly outdoors
The route

One day, readable at a glance.

Open the route in Google Maps ↗
Schedule

From arrival to the final stop.

Set your own pace. The times are indicative, not appointments. Use them to understand the shape of the day, then adjust stops, breaks and walking speed to your own pace.

  1. 09:1545 min
    parkland-walk-oxford-road

    Parkland Walk from Oxford Road

    Enter beside Finsbury Park and let the former railway establish the day’s main idea: infrastructure has not disappeared, but become the armature for an urban nature reserve.

    The reserve is normally accessible at all times. Check the Friends of Parkland Walk access page for works or diversions, especially after severe weather.

    Open this location ↗Read the linked story →

    Next: Continue west along the former track bed to the surviving platforms of Crouch End station

  2. 10:0025 min
    crouch-end-station-platforms

    Crouch End station platforms and the Spriggan

    The abandoned platforms make the railway geometry legible. Look for the Spriggan above the brick arches, but spend equal time on bridges, retaining walls and the long view along the old line.

    This is an outdoor stop on the reserve. Surfaces can be wet and the artwork is easiest to miss when vegetation is dense.

    Open this location ↗Read the linked story →

    Next: Stay on Parkland Walk to its proper end at Holmesdale Road, then use the street connection to Queen’s Wood rather than treating the closed railway tunnels as a route · 45 min

  3. 11:1050 min
    queens-wood-cafe

    Queen’s Wood and Queen’s Wood Café

    The detour is worth making: ancient oak and hornbeam replace the railway cutting, while the café in the former keeper’s lodge provides the route’s most dependable pause for an early lunch.

    The café currently advertises daily service, but opening and kitchen times can change. Check its website before relying on it for lunch.

    Open this location ↗

    Next: Walk south through Highgate towards the village and enter Waterlow Park from the northern side · 30 min

  4. 12:3045 min
    highgate-village-waterlow-park

    Highgate Village and Waterlow Park

    Use the village as a change of scale rather than a shopping stop, then cross Waterlow Park downhill. Its terraces, mature trees and city views prepare the transition from living neighbourhood to cemetery landscape.

    Waterlow Park closes at a seasonally changing time. The current closing time is posted at its gates; check Camden’s park schedule in winter.

    Open this location ↗

    Next: Leave near Swain’s Lane and walk to Highgate Cemetery’s visitor entrance · 10 min

  5. 13:2590 min
    highgate-cemetery

    Highgate Cemetery

    Choose East, West or a combined ticket according to time and availability. The essential subject is not a list of famous graves, but the changing relationship between monument, woodland and memory.

    Currently open daily 10:00–17:00 from March to October, last entry 16:30; 10:00–16:00 from November to February, last entry 15:30. Closed 25–26 December. Tickets and access rules should be checked and booked in advance.

    Open this location ↗Read the linked story →

    Next: Walk downhill and west across the lower edge of Hampstead Heath to the Parliament Hill viewpoint · 30 min

  6. 15:2535 min
    parliament-hill-viewpoint

    Parliament Hill viewpoint

    End with the protected panorama across London. The skyline is not a decorative finale: it reveals how far the route has travelled from a local railway cutting to a metropolitan viewpoint.

    The viewpoint is outdoors on Hampstead Heath and does not require a ticket. Visibility, path condition and daylight are the real constraints; Gospel Oak and Hampstead Heath stations are nearby.

    Open this location ↗

A railway that becomes a landscape

This route works because it is not a collection of unrelated Highgate attractions. It follows a sequence of landscapes in which London’s infrastructure, woodland and rituals of memory keep replacing one another: a railway becomes a nature reserve; an ancient wood interrupts the suburban street plan; a public park opens towards a cemetery; and the day ends with the entire city visible from the Heath.

Start at the Oxford Road gate beside Finsbury Park. Parkland Walk’s southern section runs for just over three kilometres to Holmesdale Road. The track has gone, but the railway remains legible in the width of the cutting, the surviving bridges, retaining walls and the platforms of the former Crouch End station. The reserve is not untouched countryside. Its habitats grew on engineered land and now depend on active management. That tension is precisely why the walk matters.

Read the old station, not only the monster

At Crouch End, the platforms are the strongest archaeological moment. The Spriggan sculpture above a brick arch has become the popular image, but it should not reduce the stop to a quick photograph. Stand between the platforms and look along the former line: the scale of the railway returns immediately.

Continue to the proper end of Parkland Walk South at Holmesdale Road. The former tunnels beyond are closed and are not a shortcut. From here the route deliberately leaves the railway and diverts north through Queen’s Wood. This is a genuine detour, not an attempt to pretend that the green corridor is continuous.

Queen’s Wood earns the diversion

Queen’s Wood changes the texture of the day. Oak and hornbeam, steep paths and a less engineered woodland floor replace the long railway cutting. The café in the old keeper’s lodge is the sensible place for an early lunch, but the wood should not be treated merely as access to food. Give it time before turning south towards Highgate.

Highgate Village then provides a short architectural interval. Do not let its shops consume the afternoon: the more interesting movement is downhill through Waterlow Park, where terraces, mature trees and changing views create a measured approach to Swain’s Lane.

Highgate Cemetery: choose depth over completion

Highgate Cemetery can absorb several hours. This itinerary gives it ninety minutes, which is enough for a focused visit but not for an exhaustive survey of East and West. Decide in advance whether your priority is the more open, biographical landscape of East or the denser architecture and processional drama of West. If a combined ticket or suitable tour is available, follow it without racing.

The piano memorial to Harry Thornton is a useful reminder that the cemetery’s strength lies in individual forms of remembrance as much as famous names. Karl Marx, George Eliot and the Egyptian Avenue attract attention, but roots, weathered lettering and the negotiation between conservation and woodland make the larger argument.

Finish by widening the scale

From Swain’s Lane, continue to Parliament Hill. The final climb asks for more effort after the cemetery, but the protected view is the right conclusion. Parkland Walk made you read the city in section—cuttings, bridges and platforms. Parliament Hill reverses the perspective and presents London as a single, distant field.

Before setting out

The route can be completed on any day, but not every interior or service is guaranteed. Confirm café service, Waterlow Park’s seasonal closing time, cemetery tickets and the current Parkland Walk access notices. Start early in winter so that the cemetery is reached well before last admission and the final paths are walked in daylight. After prolonged rain, expect mud in Parkland Walk, Queen’s Wood and the cemetery. The timings are a framework, not a demand to hurry.

Sources and verification

Hours and access can change: always check the official sources before setting out.

This is not a step-free itinerary. Parkland Walk has rough and muddy sections, the Holmesdale Road exit is steep, Queen’s Wood has uneven paths, and Highgate Cemetery includes slopes, steps and irregular surfaces.
